hook_text: Cut open a phone charger cable and you will find three very different kinds of element working together.
clip_script: In the middle: copper. A metal. Metals shine, carry electricity and heat, can be hammered flat or stretched into wire, and ring like a bell. That is why the wires are copper. Around the copper: plastic, made mostly from non-metal elements like carbon and hydrogen. Non-metals are the opposite team: dull, brittle, and they block electricity, so the plastic stops you getting shocked. Many non-metals, like oxygen, are invisible gases. And at the other end of the cable, inside your phone: silicon. A semi-metal from the staircase of the Periodic Table. Shiny like a metal, brittle like a non-metal, and it lets through just a controlled bit of electricity, perfect for billions of tiny switches on a chip. Made from ordinary sand.
visual_style: Whiteboard cutaway of a cable with labelled copper core and plastic sleeve; a hammer flattening copper and shattering sulphur; a phone opening to reveal a glowing chip.
pacing: Three crisp reveals, each with a quick property list.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort the elements in everything you use.
